newsitem.title: UK: Refinery profits hit 15-mth highs on US Gulf coast.
newsitem.headline: Refinery profits hit 15-mth highs on US Gulf coast.

text.p: Refinery profit margins on the U.S. Gulf coast edged up to 15-month highs last week, driven by surging gasoline prices, while elsewhere profits stayed buoyant just below recent highs.
Profit margins processing Brent averaged $2.85 a barrel last week, a gain of 43 cents on the previous week, according to Reuters data using standard product yields.
They hit $3.31 a barrel last Friday, the highest level since May last year, due mostly to buoyant gasoline prices which have staged an unusual late summer rally.

Gasoline climbed to about $8 a barrel above crude on NYMEX, compared to an average of $4.82 over the past year. The contra-seasonal gasoline rally was not matched in heating oil which held just $3.13 above crude, near the middle of the recently traded range.
In Europe gasoline fell sharply from five-year highs, trimming buoyant margins, but the prospect of Iraqi crude helped kept a lid on crude prices and gasoline managed a late week corrective bounce.
Profits running Brent in Rotterdam averaged $2.77 a barrel last week, a drop of seven cents from the previous week.
Despite the loss, margins remain close to historically high levels. The outlook for margins is closely tied to gasoline prices which have been volatile in recent weeks.
The crack spread between gasoline and Brent is holding above $8 a barrel on the front end of the market but sharply lower at around 43.25 a barrel for the inter-months.
In the Mediterranean, profits from fully upgrading Urals averaged $2.60 a barrel, a jump of 62 cents from the previous week.
Dealers said some of the gains reflected refiners delaying crude purchases until the impact of growing Iraqi exports is felt.
This, combined with the strong U.S. gasoline demand, helped lift profits to three-month highs mid-week although margins dipped sharply on Friday.
In Singapore profits upgrading Dubai crude gained 18 cents to average $2.09 a barrel last week, although levels fell towards the end of the week.
Margins are well below the peaks of above $6 a barrel hit last spring but well above lows hit a year ago as late summer demand for oil products dried up.
